expectedText:
MANDATORY SEXUAL HARASSMENT PREVENTION TRAINING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement under Government Code § 12950.1, as it relates to Acme Corp., which reports approximately 25 employees, and to Jane Doe. It states facts drawn from the statute's own text about which employers the statute covers, how many hours of training the statute requires and for which category of employee, how often the statute requires that training to repeat, the timing the statute sets for a new hire's or new supervisor's first training, the content categories the statute specifies, and the statute's own limits on what compliance with it does and does not establish in a harassment case.

This information sheet does not determine whether Acme Corp. is an employer the statute covers, whether Jane Doe holds a "supervisory" or "nonsupervisory" position for purposes of the statute, whether Acme Corp.'s training as actually delivered satisfies every requirement described here, or what Acme Corp. or Jane Doe should do about any of the facts it describes.

WHICH EMPLOYERS MUST COMPLY
California law requires an employer having five or more employees to provide the sexual harassment prevention training described in this information sheet. For purposes of this particular statute, an "employer" is defined to include any person who regularly employs five or more persons, or who regularly receives the services of five or more persons providing services under a contract — meaning the count that triggers this training requirement is not limited to an employer's own common-law employees — as well as any person acting as an employer's agent, the state, its political or civil subdivisions, and cities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "By January 1, 2021, an employer having five or more employees shall provide at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all supervisory employees and at least one hour of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all nonsupervisory employees in California."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the employer coverage threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "For purposes of this section only, “employer” means any person regularly employing five or more persons or regularly receiving the services of five or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state, or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(h)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the section-specific definition of "employer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  Known gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code § 12950.1 — the first from subdivision (a)(1) and the second from subdivision (h)(1), which defines "employer" only "for purposes of this section." This clause does not cover the separate, more general definition of "employer" used elsewhere in the Fair Employment and Housing Act (Government Code § 12926), which differs from this section's own definition and governs other FEHA protections, including the harassment prohibition itself, which under a separate FEHA provision (Government Code § 12940(j)) is not limited to employers of any particular size — this clause does not independently verify that separate provision's current text. This clause also does not independently verify how "regularly receiving the services of five or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract" has been construed in practice — that is a factual/interpretive question the statute's text alone does not resolve.

TWO HOURS FOR SUPERVISORY EMPLOYEES, ONE HOUR FOR NONSUPERVISORY EMPLOYEES
The statute sets a different minimum number of training hours depending on the employee's role. It requires at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment for supervisory employees, and at least one hour of the same kind of training for nonsupervisory employees. The same two-hour/one-hour division carries over to the state-developed online training courses the statute separately directs the state to make available: the online course for nonsupervisory employees is one hour long, and the online course for supervisory employees is two hours long.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "By January 1, 2021, an employer having five or more employees shall provide at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all supervisory employees and at least one hour of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all nonsupervisory employees in California."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the two-hour/one-hour split (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "The course for nonsupervisory employees shall be one hour in length and the course for supervisory employees shall be two hours in length."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the length of the state's own online training courses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  Known gap: Both quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1 — (a)(1) and (j). The statute permits the required hours to be completed individually or in a group, and in shorter segments, "as long as the applicable hourly total requirement is met" (also subdivision (a)(1), a phrase this clause does not separately quote). This clause does not define "supervisory employee"; that term is defined elsewhere in the Fair Employment and Housing Act (Government Code § 12926), which this clause does not independently fetch, quote, or verify.

TWO-YEAR RETRAINING CYCLE AND NEW-HIRE/NEW-SUPERVISOR TIMING
Once an employer has provided the initial round of training, the statute requires the employer to provide sexual harassment training and education to each covered employee again once every two years. The statute sets separate deadlines for employees who join, or are newly promoted into, a covered role between two-year cycles: a new nonsupervisory employee must be trained within six months of hire, and a new supervisory employee must be trained within six months of assuming the supervisory position.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Thereafter, each employer covered by this section shall provide sexual harassment training and education to each employee in California once every two years."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the recurring two-year training cycle (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "New nonsupervisory employees shall be provided training within six months of hire. New supervisory employees shall be provided training within six months of the assumption of a supervisory position."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the six-month deadline for new nonsupervisory and new supervisory employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  Known gap: Both quotes are from subdivision (a)(1) of Government Code § 12950.1. This clause does not cover the statute's separate, narrower timing rule for seasonal, temporary, or other employees hired to work less than six months, which — per subdivision (f), not quoted here — instead requires training within 30 calendar days of the hire date or within 100 hours worked, whichever occurs first. It also does not cover subdivision (m)'s portability rule for an employee already trained in compliance with this section by a current, prior, alternate, or joint employer within the preceding two years, nor the multiemployer-collective-bargaining-agreement construction-industry alternative in subdivision (l). The statute's own text separately notes a now-historical rule, not quoted here, that an employer who provided this training to an employee in 2019 was not required to provide refresher training to that employee again until two years thereafter.

WHAT THE TRAINING MUST COVER
The statute specifies particular content categories the training must include, beyond the hours themselves. The training must include information and practical guidance regarding the federal and state statutory provisions concerning the prohibition against, and the prevention and correction of, sexual harassment, and the remedies available to victims of sexual harassment in employment, along with practical examples aimed at instructing supervisors in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, presented by trainers or educators with knowledge and expertise in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation. Separately, the statute requires that the training include prevention of "abusive conduct" as a component, and that it include training inclusive of harassment based on gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation as a component.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The training and education required by this section shall include information and practical guidance regarding the federal and state statutory provisions concerning the prohibition against and the prevention and correction of sexual harassment and the remedies available to victims of sexual harassment in employment. The training and education shall also include practical examples aimed at instructing supervisors in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, and shall be presented by trainers or educators with knowledge and expertise in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the required general content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "An employer shall also include prevention of abusive conduct as a component of the training and education specified in paragraph (1)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the required abusive-conduct component (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "An employer shall also provide training inclusive of harassment based on gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation as a component of the training and education specified in paragraph (1)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the required gender-identity/expression and sexual-orientation component (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  Known gap: All three quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1: the first from (a)(1), the second from (a)(2), and the third from (a)(3). The statute separately defines "abusive conduct" in subdivision (h)(2), a definition this clause does not quote. This clause also does not cover subdivision (i)'s option for an employer to develop its own training module or to direct employees to the state's online course instead, nor the further detail the statute gives (in subdivision (l)(5)(B)) about what a "qualified trainer" must be able to teach when relied on under the separate multiemployer-collective-bargaining-agreement alternative in subdivision (l) — that detail is specific to that alternative and does not itself define what every employer's general training content must cover.

COMPLIANCE IS NOT A SHIELD, AND NON-COMPLIANCE IS NOT AUTOMATIC LIABILITY
The statute draws an explicit two-way line around what compliance with it proves in a harassment case. On one side, a claim that the required training did not actually reach a particular individual does not, by itself, make an employer liable to that individual in a lawsuit alleging sexual harassment. On the other side, an employer's compliance with the training requirement does not insulate the employer from liability for sexual harassment of any current or former employee or applicant. Separately, the statute gives a state agency — not the individual employee — the mechanism for enforcing the training requirement itself: if an employer violates this section, the department may seek an order requiring the employer to comply with these requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "a claim that the training and education required by this section did not reach a particular individual or individuals shall not in and of itself result in the liability of any employer to any present or former employee or applicant in any action alleging sexual harassment. Conversely, an employer’s compliance with this section does not insulate the employer from liability for sexual harassment of any current or former employee or applicant."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the limits on what a training claim proves (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  "If an employer violates this section, the department may seek an order requiring the employer to comply with these requirements."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the department's enforcement authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12950.1)
  Known gap: Both quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1 — (c) and (d). Subdivision (c) also cross-references Government Code § 12940, subdivisions (j) and (k) (the general FEHA harassment-liability and reasonable-steps provisions), which this clause does not independently fetch, quote, or verify. "The department" in subdivision (d) is not separately defined within the quoted text; the chapter heading on the fetched source page identifies the enclosing part of the Government Code as governing the "Civil Rights Department," the name given by a 2022 renaming to the same agency this chapter has long treated as its enforcing department, but this clause does not independently trace that renaming's legislative history beyond what the fetched source's own heading shows.

TRAINING RECORD AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Employer: Acme Corp.
Employee: Jane Doe
Job title: Store Manager

Role for purposes of this training (check one):
☐ Supervisory employee (at least two hours of training)
☐ Nonsupervisory employee (at least one hour of training)

Training completed on: January 1, 2026

Jane Doe acknowledges having received and completed the training and education described in this information sheet, on the date and for the role checked above.

Signature of Jane Doe: _________________________

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

[This information sheet describes Government Code § 12950.1 as codified. It does not determine that the training described above met every requirement of that statute, is not a legal opinion about Acme Corp.'s or Jane Doe's compliance with it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]
